claims.text: Superconducting behavior in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by local lattice distortions induced by atomic size mismatch rather than by variations in electron–phonon coupling when electronic concentration is approximately constant.
Elements with similar electron count but significantly different atomic radii can be substituted to increase atomic size mismatch while keeping average electron–phonon coupling nearly constant.
Pair distribution function analysis can measure local lattice distortions in the proposed alloys.
Broadening of phonon spectral features indicates increased local strain.
Atomic size mismatch introduces local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions create a random potential landscape.
The random potential landscape disrupts the uniformity of phonon modes.
The random potential landscape alters the local superconducting pairing environment.
Changes in the local superconducting pairing environment affect Tc even when average electron–phonon coupling remains unchanged.
Increasing atomic size mismatch will produce measurable shifts in Tc relative to a minimal-mismatch baseline.
The Tc shift caused by increasing atomic size mismatch will likely be a suppression.
Increasing atomic size mismatch will broaden and shift phonon spectra relative to the baseline.
Increasing atomic size mismatch will enhance indicators of local lattice distortion relative to the baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies to HEAs with isotropic s-wave, BCS-like superconductivity in the dirty limit.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when factors other than size mismatch significantly alter electron–phonon interactions.
Altered scattering rates may contribute to the observed superconducting behavior as a secondary effect.
Failure of increasing size mismatch to correlate with significant Tc changes or measurable phonon and local-structure changes relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
